text: A robot sits at the top-left of an m by n grid and moves only right or down to reach the bottom-right. How many unique paths are there?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — only two moves, right and down, no obstacles, and I count distinct paths to the exact bottom-right cell?
Correct — right and down only, grid up to a hundred by a hundred.
Got it. At most ten thousand cells, so visiting each cell once is cheap. Let me run through an example. A three by seven grid gives twenty-eight paths.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would recurse over every path, picking right or down at each step. That's exponential, and it reaches the same cells over and over. This problem reminds me of a two-D grid DP, because each cell's count depends only on its neighbors. Let dp of i, j be the number of paths to cell i, j. Since I only move right or down, I reach it either from above or from the left, so dp of i, j is the cell above plus the cell to the left. The first row and column are all one — only one straight path along an edge.

Here's the plan. One: fill the whole grid with ones, which covers the first row and column. Two: for every inner cell, add the cell above and the cell to the left. Three: return the bottom-right cell. One thing worth flagging — because each cell only needs the row above plus its left neighbor, I can drop to a single row: dp of j plus-equals dp of j minus one, scanning left to right, for order n space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

The two-D grid first. The table starts as all ones, and the double loop from index one adds up plus left. And the order n space rolling version keeps just one row. Both are order m times n time. One thing worth flagging — the rolling scan must go left to right, so dp of j minus one is already this row's value, the left neighbor, while dp of j is still last row's, the cell above. Also, its outer loop runs m times, up to and including m: the row starts as a one followed by zeros, so the first pass just builds row zero.

Let's dry-run the two-D table on a three by four grid — expected ten. The cell that matters is the corner: dp two, three is dp one, three plus dp two, two, so four plus six, ten. The rolling version produces the same rows: all ones, then one, two, three, four, then one, three, six, ten. Correct. Corner cases: a one by one grid gives one, since the start is the goal. A single row or a single column also gives one — just the straight line.

Time is order m times n, space order m times n, or order n with the rolling row. Oh, one more thing — there's also a pure-math answer: a path is a choice of which m minus one of the m plus n minus two steps go down, so it's m plus n minus two choose m minus one, in order min of m and n time. But I'd keep the DP as the template — it extends directly to grids with obstacles or with cell costs, where the closed form breaks.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You built the up-plus-left recurrence with the first row and column as the base. You compressed to one row and explained why the scan goes left to right. And you knew the combinatorial closed form but kept DP for generality. Good work.
